Judges — Book introduction (Modern English production candidate)

The book of Judges tells Israel's history during the time of the judges.

These were deliverers whom God raised up at particular times to rescue Israel from oppressors, reform the nation's religious life and administer justice to the people.

In this book, God's people appear less prosperous and less devoted to him than we might have expected.

Nevertheless, many believers remained among them, and the worship of the tabernacle continued.

This history demonstrates the repeated warnings and predictions Moses had given.

We should pay close attention to it, for it is full of important instruction.

Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesProceedings of the tribes of Judah and Simeon.1–8Hebron and other cities taken.9–20The proceedings of other tribes.21–36
Judah and Simeon begin the conquest (verses 1–8)

The Israelites knew that the war against the Canaanites had to continue after Joshua's death. What they did not know was how best to proceed.

They therefore inquired of the Lord.

God assigns work according to the strength he has given. Those who are most able should be prepared to do the most.

Judah held the first place in dignity and therefore should also stand first in duty.

Judah's effort would achieve nothing without God's blessing. Yet God would not give success while Judah refused to act.

Judah was the largest and most important tribe, while Simeon was the smallest.

Even so, Judah asked for Simeon's friendship and help.

Israelites should help one another against the Canaanites. Likewise, Christians from different groups should support and strengthen one another.

People who help each other in love have reason to hope that God will graciously assist them both.

Adoni-bezek was captured.

He had been a cruel tyrant.

The Israelites, Henry believes, acted under God's direction in making him suffer the kind of cruelty he had inflicted on others.

His own conscience acknowledged the justice of what happened to him.

God's righteousness is sometimes displayed when a sinner's punishment corresponds to the sin committed.

Hebron and other cities are taken (verses 9–20)

The Canaanites had chariots made with iron, but Israel had the Lord on its side.

His chariots are thousands of angels (Psalm 68:17).

Nevertheless, the Israelites allowed fear to overcome faith.

Caleb's actions have already been described in Joshua 15:16–19.

The Kenites also settled in the land.

Israel allowed them to live where they wished because they were a peaceful and contented people.

They troubled no one, and no one troubled them.

Blessed are the meek, for they will inherit the earth.

Other tribes leave enemies unconquered (verses 21–36)

Israel grew careless in both duty and its own long-term interests.

Out of laziness and fear, the people refused to finish conquering the land.

Greed contributed as well: they hoped to profit from allowing Canaanites to remain among them.

They did not hate or fear idolatry as they should have done.

The same unbelief that had kept their ancestors wandering for forty years now prevented them from possessing Canaan fully.

Distrusting God's power and promises deprived them of blessings and brought new troubles.

The same can happen to believers who begin their Christian lives well.

Their spiritual graces become weak, sinful desires revive, Satan attacks them through temptations suited to their character, and the world regains its influence.

Their consciences become burdened with guilt, their hearts with sorrow, their reputations with disgrace, and the gospel itself suffers dishonor.

A believer may be corrected severely and eventually restored without being lost.

Even so, the person may mourn those foolish decisions throughout life and, when approaching death, regret opportunities lost to glorify God and serve the church.

Fellowship with God's enemies, whether around us or in our own hearts, can only harm us.

Our wisdom is to continue the struggle against them without making peace with sin.
classic_reading:
[Judg.1.1-Judg.1.8]
Judges
The book of Judges is the history of Israel during the government of the Judges, who were occasional deliverers, raised up by God to rescue Israel from their oppressors, to reform the state of religion, and to administer justice to the people. The state of God's people does not appear in this book so prosperous, nor their character so religious, as might have been expected; but there were many believers among them, and the tabernacle service was attended to. The history exemplifies the frequent warnings and predictions of Moses, and should have close attention. The whole is full of important instruction.
Chapter 1
Chapter Outline
Proceedings of the tribes of Judah and Simeon. | (1-8) |
Hebron and other cities taken. | (9-20) |
The proceedings of other tribes. | (21-36) |
Verses 1-8
The Israelites were convinced that the war against the Canaanites was to be continued; but they were in doubt as to the manner in which it was to be carried on after the death of Joshua. In these respects they inquired of the Lord. God appoints service according to the strength he has given. From those who are most able, most work is expected. Judah was first in dignity, and must be first in duty. Judah's service will not avail unless God give success; but God will not give the success, unless Judah applies to the service. Judah was the most considerable of all the tribes, and Simeon the least; yet Judah begs Simeon's friendship, and prays for aid from him. It becomes Israelites to help one another against Canaanites; and all Christians, even those of different tribes, should strengthen one another. Those who thus help one another in love, have reason to hope that God will graciously help both. Adoni-bezek was taken prisoner. This prince had been a severe tyrant. The Israelites, doubtless under the Divine direction, made him suffer what he had done to others; and his own conscience confessed that he was justly treated as he had treated others. Thus the righteous God sometimes, in his providence, makes the punishment answer the sin.
[Judg.1.9-Judg.1.20]
Verses 9-20
The Canaanites had iron chariots; but Israel had God on their side, whose chariots are thousands of angels, [Ps.68.17] Psa 68:17. Yet they suffered their fears to prevail against their faith. About Caleb we read in [Josh.15.16-Josh.15.19] Jos 15:16-19. The Kenites had settled in the land. Israel let them fix where they pleased, being a quiet, contented people. They that molested none, were molested by none. Blessed are the meek, for they shall inherit the earth.
[Judg.1.21-Judg.1.36]
Verses 21-36
The people of Israel were very careless of their duty and interest. Owing to slothfulness and cowardice, they would not be at the pains to complete their conquests. It was also owing to their covetousness: they were willing to let the Canaanites live among them, that they might make advantage of them. They had not the dread and detestation of idolatry they ought to have had. The same unbelief that kept their fathers forty years out of Canaan, kept them now out of the full possession of it. Distrust of the power and promise of God deprived them of advantages, and brought them into troubles. Thus many a believer who begins well is hindered. His graces languish, his lusts revive, Satan plies him with suitable temptations, the world recovers its hold; he brings guilt into his conscience, anguish into his heart, discredit on his character, and reproach on the gospel. Though he may have sharp rebukes, and be so recovered that he does not perish, yet he will have deeply to lament his folly through his remaining days; and upon his dying bed to mourn over the opportunities of glorifying God and serving the church he has lost. We can have no fellowship with the enemies of God within us or around us, but to our hurt; therefore our only wisdom is to maintain unceasing war against them.

The angel of the Lord rebukes Israel (verses 1–5)

The One speaking to Israel was the great Angel of the covenant—the Word, the Son of God.

He spoke with divine authority as Jehovah and called the people to account for their disobedience.

The Lord reminded them both of what he had done and what he had promised.

People who turn away from fellowship with God to share in fruitless works of darkness do not understand what they are doing.

Soon they will have no excuse when called to account.

Their folly has consequences.

Those who expect to benefit from friendship with God's enemies deceive themselves.

God often allows people to experience their sin as its own punishment.

Thorns and snares lie on the path of those who stubbornly oppose him.

The people wept, recognizing their folly and ingratitude.

They trembled at God's word, and with good reason.

It is remarkable that sinners can read Scripture without tears.

If Israel had remained close to the Lord and kept its duty, the sound of its assemblies would have been joyful singing.

But through sin the people had brought themselves to tears.

Worship is naturally a matter for joy, praise and gratitude.

Our sins make weeping necessary.

It is good to weep over sin, but tears, prayers and even corrected behavior cannot atone for wrongdoing.

A new generation forgets the Lord (verses 6–23)

This passage summarizes the pattern of Israel's history during the judges.

Abandoning God made the nation weak and miserable.

Faithfulness would have made it strong and happy.

The punishment corresponded to the sin.

The Israelites worshiped the gods of surrounding nations, even the lowest of them, and God allowed the rulers of those nations to dominate them.

Anyone who has seen God keep his promises can be equally certain that he will keep his warnings.

He could have abandoned the Israelites justly.

Yet his compassion led him to raise up judges.

The Lord was with these judges, and so they became deliverers.

Even when the church experiences terrible distress, God will find or equip people to help it.

Israel, however, was not thoroughly reformed.

The people remained devoted to idols and obstinately returned to sin.

Those who abandon a way of life they once knew and professed can become increasingly bold in wrongdoing and hardened in heart.

God allowed Canaanites to remain, and Israel suffered from the very people it had chosen to tolerate.

Likewise, people cherish their corrupt desires.

God may justly leave them to the power of those desires until they become the cause of their ruin.

Scripture tells us that our hearts are deceptive and deeply wicked.

Yet we seldom believe that warning until we have recklessly approached temptation and discovered it through bitter experience.

Let us examine ourselves, pray without ceasing, be rooted in love and have Christ dwelling in our hearts through faith.

Let us declare war against every sin and pursue holiness throughout our lives.

Chapter 2
Chapter Outline
The angel of the Lord rebukes the people. | (1-5) |
The wickedness of the new generation after Joshua. | (6-23) |
Verses 1-5
It was the great Angel of the covenant, the Word, the Son of God, who spake with Divine authority as Jehovah, and now called them to account for their disobedience. God sets forth what he had done for Israel, and what he had promised. Those who throw off communion with God, and have fellowship with the unfruitful works of darkness, know not what they do now, and will have nothing to say for themselves in the day of account shortly. They must expect to suffer for this their folly. Those deceive themselves who expect advantages from friendship with God's enemies. God often makes men's sin their punishment; and thorns and snares are in the way of the froward, who will walk contrary to God. The people wept, crying out against their own folly and ingratitude. They trembled at the word, and not without cause. It is a wonder sinners can ever read the Bible with dry eyes. Had they kept close to God and their duty, no voice but that of singing had been heard in their congregation; but by their sin and folly they made other work for themselves, and nothing is to be heard but the voice of weeping. The worship of God, in its own nature, is joy, praise, and thanksgiving; our sins alone render weeping needful. It is pleasing to see men weep for their sins; but our tears, prayers, and even amendment, cannot atone for sin.
[Judg.2.6-Judg.2.23]
Verses 6-23
We have a general idea of the course of things in Israel, during the time of the Judges. The nation made themselves as mean and miserable by forsaking God, as they would have been great and happy if they had continued faithful to him. Their punishment answered to the evil they had done. They served the gods of the nations round about them, even the meanest, and God made them serve the princes of the nations round about them, even the meanest. Those who have found God true to his promises, may be sure that he will be as true to his threatenings. He might in justice have abandoned them, but he could not for pity do it. The Lord was with the judges when he raised them up, and so they became saviours. In the days of the greatest distress of the church, there shall be some whom God will find or make fit to help it. The Israelites were not thoroughly reformed; so mad were they upon their idols, and so obstinately bent to backslide. Thus those who have forsaken the good ways of God, which they have once known and professed, commonly grow most daring and desperate in sin, and have their hearts hardened. Their punishment was, that the Canaanites were spared, and so they were beaten with their own rod. Men cherish and indulge their corrupt appetites and passions; therefore God justly leaves them to themselves, under the power of their sins, which will be their ruin. God has told us how deceitful and desperately wicked our hearts are, but we are not willing to believe it, until by making bold with temptation we find it true by sad experience. We need to examine how matters stand with ourselves, and to pray without ceasing, that we may be rooted and grounded in love, and that Christ may dwell in our hearts by faith. Let us declare war against every sin, and follow after holiness all our days.

Nations left to test Israel (verses 1–7)

Israel was a picture of God's church on earth.

The people were not meant to live carelessly or lazily.

The Lord allowed some of the Canaanite nations to remain so that Israel's faith would be tested.

Temptations and trials expose the wickedness in sinners' hearts.

They also strengthen the graces of believers as they struggle each day against Satan, sin and this evil world.

Christians must live within the world, but they do not belong to it and must not adopt its sinful patterns.

This distinguishes Christ's followers from people who merely profess faith.

Friendship with the world is more deadly than the world's hostility.

Hostility can kill the body, but worldly friendship has destroyed many precious souls.

Othniel delivers Israel (verses 8–11)

Othniel was the first judge.

He had already become known during Joshua's lifetime.

Soon after Israel settled in Canaan, the nation's purity was corrupted and its peace disturbed.

Suffering can make people cry out to God when they had scarcely spoken to him before.

The Lord returned to them in mercy and raised up a deliverer.

The Spirit of the Lord came upon Othniel.

The Spirit gave him wisdom and courage to fit him for the task, and power to move him to perform it.

Othniel first governed Israel, rebuked its sins and worked for its reform.

Only then did he go to war.

Let us first conquer the sin within us, the worst enemy of all.

Then it will be easier to face outward enemies.

Let Christ be our Judge and Lawgiver, and he will save us.

Ehud delivers Israel from Eglon (verses 12–30)

Israel sinned again, and God raised up another oppressor.

The Israelites did wrong, and the Moabites did even worse.

Yet because God corrects his own people in this life, Israel grew weaker and Moab stronger against it.

If small troubles do not bring repentance, God may send greater ones.

When Israel prayed again, the Lord raised up Ehud.

As a judge carrying out divine justice, Ehud killed Eglon, king of Moab.

Henry understands this act as the execution of God's judgment against an enemy of the Lord and his people.

But he immediately makes an essential distinction.

Our rule today is to obey rulers and authorities in everything that is lawful. No such special commissions are given now. Claiming one would be blasphemy against God.

Ehud's words to Eglon remind us that a proud rebel can expect a message of judgment from God.

Scripture contains such a warning.

Ministers must declare it boldly, neither fearing the anger of sinners nor showing favoritism.

But blessed be God, his ministers also bring a message of mercy and free salvation.

The warning of judgment is for people who reject God's gracious offer.

After Ehud's victory, the land had peace for eighty years.

That was a long rest, but it cannot compare with the everlasting rest of the saints in the heavenly Canaan.

Shamgar delivers Israel (verse 31)

The Philistines threatened the southwestern region.

The Lord raised up Shamgar to deliver it.

Without a sword or spear, Shamgar took the nearest available tool—an oxgoad.

God can use people for his glory and the good of his church even when their birth, education or occupation seem humble and obscure.

The weapon itself is not what matters if God directs and strengthens the person using it.

He often works through unlikely means so that everyone can see the excellence of his power.

As the Israelites were a type of the church on earth, they were not to be idle and slothful. The Lord was pleased to try them by the remains of the devoted nations they spared. Temptations and trials detect the wickedness of the hearts of sinners; and strengthen he graces of believers in their daily conflict with Satan, sin, and this evil world. They must live in this world, but they are not of it, and are forbidden to conform to it. This marks the difference between the followers of Christ and mere professors. The friendship of the world is more fatal than its enmity; the latter can only kill the body, but the former murders many precious souls.
[Judg.3.8-Judg.3.11]
Verses 8-11
The first judge was Othniel: even in Joshua's time Othniel began to be famous. Soon after Israel's settlement in Canaan their purity began to be corrupted, and their peace disturbed. But affliction makes those cry to God who before would scarcely speak to him. God returned in mercy to them for their deliverance. The Spirit of the Lord came upon Othniel. The Spirit of wisdom and courage to qualify him for the service, and the Spirit of power to excite him to it. He first judged Israel, reproved and reformed them, and then went to war. Let sin at home be conquered, that worst of enemies, then enemies abroad will be more easily dealt with. Thus let Christ be our Judge and Lawgiver, then he will save us.
[Judg.3.12-Judg.3.30]
Verses 12-30
When Israel sins again, God raises up a new oppressor. The Israelites did ill, and the Moabites did worse; yet because God punishes the sins of his own people in this world, Israel is weakened, and Moab strengthened against them. If lesser troubles do not do the work, God will send greater. When Israel prays again, God raises up Ehud. As a judge, or minister of Divine justice, Ehud put to death Eglon, the king of Moab, and thus executed the judgments of God upon him as an enemy to God and Israel. But the law of being subject to principalities and powers in all things lawful, is the rule of our conduct. No such commissions are now given; to pretend to them is to blaspheme God. Notice Ehud's address to Eglon. What message from God but a message of vengeance can a proud rebel expect? Such a message is contained in the word of God; his ministers are boldly to declare it, without fearing the frown, or respecting the persons of sinners. But, blessed be God, they have to deliver a message of mercy and of free salvation; the message of vengeance belongs only to those who neglect the offers of grace. The consequence of this victory was, that the land had rest eighty years. It was a great while for the land to rest; yet what is that to the saints' everlasting rest in the heavenly Canaan.
[Judg.3.31]
Verse 31
The side of the country which lay south-west, was infested by the Philistines. God raised up Shamgar to deliver them; having neither sword nor spear, he took an ox-goad, the instrument next at hand. God can make those serviceable to his glory and to his church's good, whose birth, education, and employment, are mean and obscure. It is no matter what the weapon is, if God directs and strengthens the arm. Often he works by unlikely means, that the excellency of the power may appear to be of God.

Israel falls under Jabin's oppression (verses 1–3)

The land had enjoyed peace for eighty years.

That long period should have strengthened Israel's faith.

Instead, prosperity made the people feel secure and indulge their sinful desires.

In that way, the prosperity of fools becomes their destruction.

Jabin and his general, Sisera, oppressed Israel severely.

This enemy was nearer than the former oppressors.

Distress finally made the Israelites cry out to the Lord, because they could see no other possibility of relief.

People who ignore God while prosperous may find themselves compelled to seek him when trouble comes.

Deborah calls Barak to deliver Israel (verses 4–9)

Deborah was a prophetess.

The Holy Spirit had instructed her in divine knowledge.

She judged Israel as God's messenger, correcting abuses and setting right the people's grievances.

At the Lord's direction, she told Barak to gather an army and confront Jabin's forces.

Barak insisted that Deborah accompany him.

She agreed.

She would not send him into danger while refusing to go there herself.

Those who call others to do their duty in God's name should be prepared to assist them.

Barak cared more about assurance of mind and success in his calling than about receiving personal honor.

Barak defeats Sisera (verses 10–16)

Sisera placed his confidence chiefly in his chariots.

But if we have reason to believe that God goes before us, we can proceed cheerfully and courageously.

Do not be dismayed by difficulties in resisting Satan, serving God or suffering for him.

Has the Lord not gone ahead of you?

Then follow him faithfully.

Barak went down from the mountain to the plain, although Sisera's iron chariots would have an advantage there.

Barak left the favorable ground because he was trusting in God's power.

Salvation belongs to the Lord alone (Jeremiah 3:23).

His trust was not disappointed.

When God goes before us in spiritual conflict, we must still exert ourselves.

And when he graciously grants success over the enemies of our souls, we should use that victory as encouragement to remain watchful and resolute.

Sisera is killed by Jael (verses 17–24)

Sisera's chariots had been his pride and confidence.

Such confidence in created things is doomed to disappointment.

What we lean upon may prove like a broken reed that not only gives way but wounds us.

An idol can soon become a burden (Isaiah 46:1).

God can make us weary of what we once desperately wanted.

Henry thinks Jael probably intended to show kindness to Sisera at first.

He believes that afterward a special divine impulse led her to recognize Sisera as a determined enemy of the Lord and his people and to kill him.

This is Henry's interpretation of the exceptional historical event, not a model for private violence.

We must break off associations with God's enemies if we want the Lord to be our God and his people our people.

Sisera intended to destroy Israel with many iron chariots.

Yet he himself was killed with a single iron tent peg.

Thus God uses weak things to confound the strong.

Israel would have avoided much harm if the people had earlier removed the Canaanites as God had commanded and enabled them.

Yet it is better to become wise late, through painful experience, than never to learn wisdom at all.

Siser's confidence was chiefly in his chariots. But if we have ground to hope that God goes before us, we may go on with courage and cheerfulness. Deborah and Barak praise the Lord (verses 1–5)

We should waste no time thanking the Lord for his mercies.

Praise is most acceptable to him and most helpful to us when it rises from a full heart.

Thanksgiving strengthens and deepens believers' love and gratitude.

It also makes God's wonderful acts more widely known and remembered for longer.

Whatever Deborah, Barak or the army had accomplished, the Lord must receive all the praise.

The will to act, the power to perform and the success achieved all came from him.

Israel's suffering and deliverance (verses 6–11)

Deborah described Israel's misery under Jabin so that its deliverance would appear all the more gracious.

She identified the cause of the suffering: idolatry.

Israel had chosen new gods with new names.

But behind those images, Henry says, the people were in fact serving Satan.

Deborah had been a mother to Israel by diligently seeking the people's spiritual welfare.

She called everyone who benefited from their great deliverance to thank the Lord.

Those who regained their freedom and position should praise God for that restoration.

The Lord himself accomplished it.

In judging his enemies, he also displayed his righteousness.

During persecution, attending the worship God has appointed may place a believer's life in danger.

Satan always tries to keep believers from approaching the throne of grace, the fountain of life's water.

Notice also God's tenderness toward frightened people.

His glory includes protecting those most exposed to danger and helping the weakest.

Let us value public peace, especially the safety enjoyed by those living in villages, and thank God for it.

Courage commended; indifference condemned (verses 12–23)

Deborah called upon her own soul to awaken and praise God.

Anyone who hopes to kindle love for Christ in others must first be burning with that love.

Praise is a task to which we should awaken both ourselves and our affections.

She described three groups: those who fought against Israel, those who fought for Israel, and those who kept away.

The enemies were stubborn and dangerous opponents of God's people.

The tribes that fought for Israel deserved honor.

God must receive the highest praise, but the people who serve him well should also be acknowledged, so others will be encouraged.

Indeed, the whole creation is against those who have made God their enemy.

The River Kishon fought against Sisera's forces.

Usually it was shallow, but Henry considers it likely that heavy rain had made it deep and powerful, drowning those who attempted to cross.

Deborah herself was earnestly engaged in the struggle.

When our souls become deeply involved in worship and holy duties, God's grace helps us overcome spiritual enemies.

Other tribes failed to help when their aid was needed.

Many people are held back from duty by fear of trouble, love of ease, and excessive concern for business or wealth.

Selfish people scarcely care what happens to the church so long as they can earn, keep and save money.

All seek their own interests (Philippians 2:21).

Those reluctant to serve can always find excuses for staying at home when an undertaking is dangerous or difficult.

But we cannot remain neutral in the conflict between the Lord and his enemies.

Even though God needs no human help, he accepts the service of those who employ their gifts in his cause, and he calls everyone to do so.

Jael is praised; Sisera's mother waits in vain (verses 24–31)

Jael received a special blessing.

People whose lives are spent in a small or humble setting will not lose their reward if they faithfully serve God with the gifts and opportunities they have.

Sisera's mother waited confidently for her son's return.

She had no thought that his campaign could have failed.

Her anxious hopes concerned worldly triumph and the display of greatness.

We should beware of setting our hearts on temporal advantages, especially those that feed pride and empty glory.

What a picture her wishes give of a heart ruled by worldly appetite!

The old mother's hopes and the attendants' speculations were foolish and shameful.

God can bring ruin upon his enemies precisely when they feel most confident and proud.

Deborah ended by praying for the defeat of all God's enemies and the well-being of everyone who loves him.

Those who sincerely love the Lord will finally shine like the sun in all its brightness.

Praising God is a work we should awake to, and awake ourselves unto. She notices who fought against Israel, who fought for them, and who kept away. Who fought against them. They were obstinate enemies to God's people, therefore the more dangerous. Who fought for them. At most times it was shallow, yet now, probably by the great rain that fell, it was so swelled, and the stream so deep and strong, that those who attempted to pass, were drowned. The mother of Sisera looked for his return, not in the least fearing his success. God arranged matters so that all the praise for the coming victory would belong to him alone.

Gideon's name had already filled the Midianites with fear.

God chooses what seems foolish in the world's eyes to humble the wise.

The gospel is a sword not held in a hand but proclaimed from a mouth.

People unwilling to risk anything in God's cause may be the first to criticize those who serve with greater zeal and courage.

Those most reluctant to undertake difficult work can also be the most offended when they do not receive credit for it.

Gideon gave a remarkable example of self-denial.

He showed that humility is the best answer to envy.

The Ephraimites expressed their anger in excessive and improper words.

Their bitter language showed how weak their complaint really was: when scolding grows louder, reasoning often grows weaker.

They were weary from what they had done, yet eager to continue the campaign.

This is often the experience of a true Christian.

A believer may feel faint and yet keep striving.

The world understands little of the long struggle faithful believers maintain against the sin in their own hearts.

The strength that enabled them to begin came from God.

They must continue trusting that same divine strength, because only through him can the conflict end in victory.

Succoth and Penuel are punished (verses 13–17)

Active servants of the Lord can meet more dangerous opposition from people who merely profess faith than from open enemies.

They must not let the conduct of Israelites in name but Midianites in heart discourage them.

Even when ready to faint from inward struggles and outward hardship, they should pursue the enemies of their souls and of God's work.

The Lord will give them strength to persevere.

The less help people offer—and the more they try to hinder—the more God's assistance may become evident.

The resulting punishment was just.

Many people learn through the thorns of affliction because they would not learn in any gentler way.

The kings of Midian had to answer for the killing of Gideon's brothers.

They acknowledged that they had committed murder.

Gideon acted as the avenger of blood, being the nearest relative of those who were killed.

The kings had not expected to be confronted about these crimes so long afterward.

Yet murder seldom goes entirely unpunished, even in this life.

Sins people have forgotten must still be accounted for before God.

What poor comfort it is to hope that death may involve less pain or disgrace than someone else's death!

Many people worry more about those things than about the coming judgment and what follows it.

Gideon refused the position of ruler offered by the people.

No good person should be pleased by receiving honor that belongs to God alone.

Gideon wanted the great victory to be remembered.

He therefore made an ephod from the finest spoils.

Henry thinks it probable that this ephod was associated with a teraphim and that Gideon intended it to be consulted as an oracle.

A single wrong decision by a good person can lead many others into false practices.

Following God's example, let us resolve not to be overcome by evil but to overcome evil with good.

Abimelech murders his brethren, and is made king. | (1-6) |
Jotham rebukes the Shechemites. | (7-21) |
The Shechemites conspire against Abimelech. | (22-29) |
Abimelech destroys Shechem. | (30-49) |
Abimelech slain. | (50-57) |
Verses 1-6
The men of Shechem chose Abimelech king. God was not consulted whether they should have any king, much less who it should be. If parents could see what their children would do, and what they are to suffer, their joy in them often would be turned into sorrow: we may be thankful that we cannot know what shall happen. Above all, we should fear and watch against sin; for our evil conduct may produce fatal effects upon our families, after we are in our graves.
[Judg.9.7-Judg.9.21]
Verses 7-21
There was no occasion for the trees to choose a king, they are all the trees of the Lord which he has planted. Nor was there any occasion for Israel to set a king over them, for the Lord was their King. Those who bear fruit for the public good, are justly respected and honoured by all that are wise, more than those who merely make a figure. All these fruit-trees gave much the same reason for their refusal to be promoted over the trees; or, as the margin reads it, to go up and down for the trees. To rule, involves a man in a great deal both of toil and care. Those who are preferred to public trust and power, must forego all private interests and advantages, for the good of others. And those advanced to honour and dignity, are in great danger of losing their fruitfulness. For which reason, they that desire to do good, are afraid of being too great. Jotham compares Abimelech to the bramble or thistle, a worthless plant, whose end is to be burned. Such a one was Abimelech.
[Judg.9.22-Judg.9.29]
Verses 22-29
Abimelech is seated in the throne his father refused. But how long does this glory last? Stay but three years, and see the bramble withered and burned. The prosperity of the wicked is short and fickle. The Shechemites are plagued by no other hand than Abimelech's. They raised him unjustly to the throne; they first feel the weight of his sceptre.
[Judg.9.30-Judg.9.49]
Verses 30-49
Abimelech intended to punish the Schechemites for slighting him now, but God punished them for their serving him formerly in the murder of Gideon's sons. When God uses men as instruments in his hand to do his work, he means one thing, and they another. That, which they hoped would have been for their welfare, proved a snare and a trap, as those will certainly find, who run to idols for shelter; such will prove a refuge of lies. (Jdg 9:50-57)
[Judg.9.50-Judg.9.57]
Verses 50-57
The Shechemites were ruined by Abimelech; now he is reckoned with, who was their leader in villany. Evil pursues sinners, and sometimes overtakes them, when not only at ease, but triumphant. Though wickedness may prosper a while, it will not prosper always. The history of mankind, if truly told, would greatly resemble that of this chapter. The records of what are called splendid events present to us such contests for power. Such scenes, though praised of men, fully explain the Scripture doctrine of the deceitfulness and desperate wickedness of the human heart, the force of men's lust, and the effect of Satan's influence. Lord, thou has given us thy word of truth and righteousness, O pour upon us thy spirit of purity, peace, and love, and write thy holy law in our hearts.

Tola and Jair govern Israel (verses 1–5)

Peaceful periods of government give historians less to write about, even though they are often the best times in which to live.

Such were the days of Tola and Jair.

They were humble, energetic and useful men, appointed by God to govern.

Philistines and Ammonites oppress Israel (verses 6–9)

God's warning now came true: Israel would be unable to stand against its enemies (Leviticus 26:17, 37).

Through their own sinful ways and actions, the people had brought this misery upon themselves.

Israel turns toward God (verses 10–18)

God can multiply punishments to correspond with the number of people's sins and idols.

But hope remains when sinners cry to the Lord for help and grieve over both their open wrongdoing and their deeper ungodliness.

True repentance requires recognizing that whatever we have placed alongside God as an object of trust cannot save us.

Israel acknowledged what the people deserved but begged God not to treat them according to that desert.

We must submit to God's justice while hoping in his mercy.

Repentance means not merely being sorry for sin, but turning away from it.

Just as a loving father is grieved by the disobedience and suffering of a child, God is grieved by the wrongdoing of his people.

No one seeks his mercy in vain.

The trembling sinner and the believer who has nearly despaired after falling away should stop debating God's hidden purposes.

Nor should they demand encouragement from their earlier religious experiences before daring to hope.

Instead, let them throw themselves upon the mercy of God our Savior.

Let them humble themselves before him, seek freedom from the powers of darkness, separate from sin and its temptations, diligently use the means of grace and wait for the Lord's appointed time.

Then they will surely rejoice in his mercy.

[Judg.10.1-Judg.10.5]
Chapter 10
Chapter Outline
Tola and Jair judge Israel. | (1-5) |
The Philistines and Ammonites oppress Israel. | (6-9) |
Israel's repentance. | (10-18) |
Verses 1-5
Quiet and peaceable reigns, though the best to live in, yield least variety of matter to be spoken of. Such were the days of Tola and Jair. They were humble, active, and useful men, rulers appointed of God.
[Judg.10.6-Judg.10.9]
Verses 6-9
Now the threatening was fulfilled, that the Israelites should have no power to stand before their enemies, [Lev.26.17] Le 26:17, [Lev.26.37] 37. By their evil ways and their evil doings they procured this to themselves.
[Judg.10.10-Judg.10.18]
Verses 10-18
God is able to multiply men's punishments according to the numbers of their sins and idols. But there is hope when sinners cry to the Lord for help, and lament their ungodliness as well as their more open transgressions. It is necessary, in true repentance, that there be a full conviction that those things cannot help us which we have set in competition with God. They acknowledged what they deserved, yet prayed to God not to deal with them according to their deserts. We must submit to God's justice, with a hope in his mercy. True repentance is not only for sin, but from sin. As the disobedience and misery of a child are a grief to a tender father, so the provocations of God's people are a grief to him. From him mercy never can be sought in vain. Let then the trembling sinner, and the almost despairing backslider, cease from debating about God's secret purposes, or from expecting to find hope from former experiences. Let them cast themselves on the mercy of God our Saviour, humble themselves under his hand, seek deliverance from the powers of darkness, separate themselves from sin, and from occasions of it, use the means of grace diligently, and wait the Lord's time, and so they shall certainly rejoice in his mercy.
